entries.1ebd6c7868ec8274cdc66325472e5a3ee3ea1ae6: <div sID="gen7748" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="1Chr.12" sID="1Chr.12"/> <div eID="gen7748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7749" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7750" type="x-p"/> What the mighty men did towards making David king we read in the foregoing chapter. Here we are told what the many did towards it. It was not all at once, but gradually, that David ascended the throne. His kingdom was to last; and therefore, like fruits that keep longest, it ripened slowly. After he had long waited for the vacancy of the throne, it was at two steps and those above seven years distant, that he ascended it. Now we are here told, I. What help came in to him to Ziklag, to make him king of Judah, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.1-1Chr.12.22">ver. 1-22</reference>. II. What help came in to him in Hebron, to make him king over all Israel, above seven years after, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.23-1Chr.12.40">ver. 23-40</reference>.
entries.24dbbdb6b800a9dd760b4624bd90f26e171fc96c: <div eID="gen7750" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7749" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Army. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1055.)</title> <div sID="gen7751" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now these <hi type="italic">are</hi> they that came to David to Ziklag, while he yet kept himself close because of Saul the son of Kish: and they <hi type="italic">were</hi> among the mighty men, helpers of the war. <hi type="super">2</hi> <hi type="italic">They were</hi> armed with bows, and could use both the right hand and the left in <hi type="italic">hurling</hi> stones and <hi type="italic">shooting</hi> arrows out of a bow, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of Saul's brethren of Benjamin. <hi type="super">3</hi> The chief <hi type="italic">was</hi> Ahiezer, then Joash, the sons of Shemaah the Gibeathite; and Jeziel, and Pelet, the sons of Azmaveth; and Berachah, and Jehu the Antothite, <hi type="super">4</hi> And Ismaiah the Gibeonite, a mighty man among the thirty, and over the thirty; and Jeremiah, and Jahaziel, and Johanan, and Josabad the Gederathite, <hi type="super">5</hi> Eluzai, and Jerimoth, and Bealiah, and Shemariah, and Shephatiah the Haruphite, <hi type="super">6</hi> Elkanah, and Jesiah, and Azareel, and Joezer, and Jashobeam, the Korhites, <hi type="super">7</hi> And Joelah, and Zebadiah, the sons of Jeroham of Gedor. <hi type="super">8</hi> And of the Gadites there separated themselves unto David into the hold to the wilderness men of might, <hi type="italic">and</hi> men of war <hi type="italic">fit</hi> for the battle, that could handle shield and buckler, whose faces <hi type="italic">were like</hi> the faces of lions, and <hi type="italic">were</hi> as swift as the roes upon the mountains; <hi type="super">9</hi> Ezer the first, Obadiah the second, Eliab the third, <hi type="super">10</hi> Mishmannah the fourth, Jeremiah the fifth, <hi type="super">11</hi> Attai the sixth, Eliel the seventh, <hi type="super">12</hi> Johanan the eighth, Elzabad the ninth, <hi type="super">13</hi> Jeremiah the tenth, Machbanai the eleventh. <hi type="super">14</hi> These <hi type="italic">were</hi> of the sons of Gad, captains of the host: one of the least <hi type="italic">was</hi> over a hundred, and the greatest over a thousand. <hi type="super">15</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> they that went over Jordan in the first month, when it had overflown all his banks; and they put to flight all <hi type="italic">them</hi> of the valleys, <hi type="italic">both</hi> toward the east, and toward the west. <hi type="super">16</hi> And there came of the children of Benjamin and Judah to the hold unto David. <hi type="super">17</hi> And David went out to meet them, and answered and said unto them, If ye be come peaceably unto me to help me, mine heart shall be knit unto you: but if <hi type="italic">ye be come</hi> to betray me to mine enemies, seeing <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no wrong in mine hands, the God of our fathers look <hi type="italic">thereon,</hi> and rebuke <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">18</hi> Then the spirit came upon Amasai, <hi type="italic">who was</hi> chief of the captains, <hi type="italic">and he said,</hi> Thine <hi type="italic">are we,</hi> David, and on thy side, thou son of Jesse: peace, peace <hi type="italic">be</hi> unto thee, and peace <hi type="italic">be</hi> to thine helpers; for thy God helpeth thee. Then David received them, and made them captains of the band. <hi type="super">19</hi> And there fell <hi type="italic">some</hi> of Manasseh to David, when he came with the Philistines against Saul to battle: but they helped them not: for the lords of the Philistines upon advisement sent him away, saying, He will fall to his master Saul to <hi type="italic">the jeopardy of</hi> our heads. <hi type="super">20</hi> As he went to Ziklag, there fell to him of Manasseh, Adnah, and Jozabad, and Jediael, and Michael, and Jozabad, and Elihu, and Zilthai, captains of the thousands that <hi type="italic">were</hi> of Manasseh. <hi type="super">21</hi> And they helped David against the band <hi type="italic">of the rovers:</hi> for they <hi type="italic">were</hi> all mighty men of valour, and were captains in the host. <hi type="super">22</hi> For at <hi type="italic">that</hi> time day by day there came to David to help him, until <hi type="italic">it was</hi> a great host, like the host of God. <div eID="gen7751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7752" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of those that appeared and acted as David's friends, upon the death of Saul, to bring about the revolution. All the forces he had, while he was persecuted, was but 600 men, who served for his guards; but, when the time had come that he must begin to act offensively, Providence brought in more to his assistance. Even while he <hi type="italic">kept himself close, because of Saul</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.1">v. 1</reference>), while he did not appear, to invite or encourage his friends and well-wishers to come in to him (not foreseeing that the death of Saul was so near), God was inclining and preparing them to come over to him with seasonable succours. Those that trust God to do his work for them in his own way and time shall find his providence outdoing all their forecast and contrivance. The war was God's, and he found out helpers of the war, whose forwardness to act for the man God designed for the government is here recorded to their honour. <div eID="gen7752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7753" type="x-p"/> I. Some, even of Saul's brethren, of the tribe of Benjamin, and a-kin to him, came over to David, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.2">v. 2</reference>. What moved them to it we are not told. Probably a generous indignation at the base treatment which Saul, one of their tribe, gave him, animated them to appear the more vigorously for him, that the guilt and reproach of it might not lie upon them. These Benjamites are described to be men of great dexterity, that were trained up in shooting and slinging, and used both hands alike—ingenious active men; a few of these might do David a great deal of service. Several of the leading men of them are here named. See <reference osisRef="Judg.20.16">Judg. xx. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen7753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7754" type="x-p"/> II. Some of the tribe of Gad, though seated on the other side Jordan, had such a conviction of David's title to the government, and fitness for it, that they <hi type="italic">separated themselves from their brethren</hi> (a laudable separation it was) to go to David, though he was <hi type="italic">in the hold in the wilderness</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.8">v. 8</reference>), probably some of his strong holds in the wilderness of Engedi. They were but few, eleven in all, here named, but they added much to David's strength. Those that had hitherto come in to his assistance were most of them men of broken fortunes, distressed, discontented, and soldiers of fortune, that came to him rather for protection than to do him any service, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.2">1 Sam. xxii. 2</reference>. But these Gadites were brave men, <hi type="italic">men of war, and fit for the battle,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.8">v. 8</reference>. For, 1. They were <hi type="italic">able-bodied men,</hi> men of incredible swiftness, not to fly from, but to fly upon, the enemy, and to pursue the scattered forces. In this they were <hi type="italic">as swift as the roes upon the mountains,</hi> so that no man could escape from them; and yet they had <hi type="italic">faces like the faces of lions,</hi> so that no man could out-fight them. 2. They were disciplined men, trained up to military exercises; they could handle shield and buckler, use both offensive and defensive weapons. 3. They were officers of the militia in their own tribe (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.14">v. 14</reference>), so that though they did not bring soldiers with them they had them at command, hundreds, thousands. 4. They were daring men, that could break through the greatest difficulties. Upon some expedition or other, perhaps this to David, they swam over the Jordan, when it <hi type="italic">overflowed all its banks,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.15">v. 15</reference>. Those are fit to be employed in the cause of God that can venture thus in a dependence upon the divine protection. 5. They were men that would go through with the business they engaged in. What enemies those were that they met with in the valleys, when they had passed Jordan, does not appear; but they put them to flight with their lion-like faces, and pursued them with matchless fury, both <hi type="italic">towards the east and towards the west;</hi> which way soever they turned, they followed their blow, and did not do their work by halves. <div eID="gen7754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7755" type="x-p"/> III. Some of Judah and Benjamin came to him, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.16">v. 16</reference>. Their leader was Amasai, whether the same with that Amasa that afterwards sided with Absalom (<reference osisRef="2Sam.17.25">2 Sam. xvii. 25</reference>) or no does not appear. Now here we have, <div eID="gen7755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7756" type="x-p"/> 1. David's prudent treaty with them, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.17">v. 17</reference>. He was surprised to see them, and could not but conceive some jealousy of the intentions of their coming, having been so often in danger by the treachery of the men of Ziph and the men of Keilah, who yet were all men of Judah. He might well be timorous whose life was so much struck at; he might well be suspicious who had been deceived in so many that he said, in his haste, <hi type="italic">All men are liars.</hi> No marvel that he meets these men of Judah with caution. Observe, <div eID="gen7756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7757" type="x-p"/> (1.) How he puts the matter to themselves, how fairly he deals with them. As they are, they shall find him; so shall all that deal with the Son of David. [1.] If they be faithful and honourable, he will be their rewarder: "<hi type="italic">If you have come peaceably unto me, to help me,</hi> though you have come late and have left me exposed a great while, though you bring no great strength with you to turn the scale for me, yet I will thankfully accept your good-will, and <hi type="italic">my heart shall be knit unto you;</hi> I will love you and honour you, and do you all the kindness I can." Affection, respect, and service, that are cordial and sincere, will find favour with a good man, as they do with a good God, though clogged with infirmities, and turning to no great account. But, [2.] If they be false, and come to betray him into the hands of Saul, under colour of friendship, he leaves them to God to be their avenger, as he is, and will be, of every thing that is treacherous and perfidious. Never was man more violently run upon, and run down, than David was (except the Son of David himself), and yet he had the testimony of his conscience that there was no wrong in his hands. He meant no harm to any man, which was his rejoicing in the day of evil, and enabled him, when he feared treachery, to commit his cause to him that judges righteously. He will not be judge in his own cause, though a wise man, nor avenge himself, though a man of valour; but let the righteous God, who hath said, <hi type="italic">Vengeance is mine,</hi> do both. <hi type="italic">The God of our fathers look thereon and rebuke it.</hi> <div eID="gen7757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7758" type="x-p"/> (2.) In this appeal observe, [1.] He calls God the <hi type="italic">God of our fathers,</hi> both his fathers and theirs. Thus he reminded them not to deal ill with him; for they were both descendants from the same patriarchs, and both dependents on the same God. Thus he encouraged himself to believe that God would right him if he should be abused; for he was the <hi type="italic">God of his fathers</hi> and therefore a blessing was entailed on him, and a God to all Israel and therefore not only a Judge to all the earth, but particularly concerned in determining controversies between contesting Israelites. [2.] He does not imprecate any fearful judgement upon them, though they should deal treacherously, but very modestly refers his cause to the divine wisdom and justice: The Lord <hi type="italic">look thereon,</hi> and judge as he sees (for he sees men's hearts), and <hi type="italic">rebuke it.</hi> It becomes those that appeal to God to express themselves with great temper and moderation; for the wrath of man <hi type="italic">works not the righteousness of God.</hi> <div eID="gen7758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7759" type="x-p"/> 2. Their hearty closure with him, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.18">v. 18</reference>. Amasai was their spokesman, on whom the <hi type="italic">Spirit of the Lord came,</hi> not a spirit of prophecy, but a spirit of wisdom and resolution, according to the occasion, putting words into his mouth, unpremeditated, which were proper both to give David satisfaction and to animate those that accompanied him. Nothing could be said finer, more lively, or more pertinent to the occasion. For himself and all his associates, (1.) He professed a very cordial adherence to David, and his interest, against all that opposed him, and a resolution to stand by him with the hazard of all that was dear to him: <hi type="italic">Thine are we, David, and on thy side, thou son of Jesse.</hi> In calling him <hi type="italic">son of Jesse</hi> they reminded themselves that he was lineally descended from Nahshon and Salmon, who in their days were princes of the tribe of Judah. Saul called him so in disdain (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.27">1 Sam. xx. 27</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.7">xxii. 7</reference>), but they looked upon it as his honour. They were convinced that God was on his side; and therefore, <hi type="italic">Thine are we, David, and on thy side.</hi> It is good, if we must side, to side with those that side with God and have God with them. (2.) He wished prosperity to David and his cause, not drinking a health, but praying for peace to him and all his friends and well-wishers: "<hi type="italic">Peace, peace, be unto thee,</hi> all the good thy heart desires, and <hi type="italic">peace be to thy helpers,</hi> among whom we desire to be reckoned, that peace may be on us." (3.) He assured him of help from heaven: "<hi type="italic">For thy God helpeth thee;</hi> therefore we wish peace may be, and therefore we doubt not but peace shall be, to thee and thy helpers. God is thy God, and those that have him for their God no doubt have him for their helper in every time of need and danger." From these expressions of Amasai we may take instruction how to testify our affection and allegiance to the Lord Jesus. His we must be without reservation or power of revocation. On his side we must be forward to appear and act. To his interest we must be hearty well-wishers: "Hosanna! prosperity to his gospel and kingdom;" for his God helpeth him, and will till he shall have put down all opposing rule, principality, and power. <div eID="gen7759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7760" type="x-p"/> 3. David's cheerful acceptance of them into his interest and friendship. Charity and honour teach us to let fall our jealousies as soon as satisfaction is given us: <hi type="italic">David received them,</hi> and preferred them to be <hi type="italic">captains of the band.</hi> <div eID="gen7760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7761" type="x-p"/> IV. Some of Manasseh likewise joined with him, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.19">v. 19</reference>. Providence gave them a fair opportunity to do so when he and his men marched through their country upon this occasion. Achish took David with him when he went out to fight with Saul; but the lords of the Philistines obliged him to withdraw. We have the story, <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.4-1Sam.29.11">1 Sam. xxix. 4</reference>, &c. In his return some great men of Manasseh, who had no heart to join with Saul against the Philistines struck in with David, and very seasonably, to help him <hi type="italic">against the band of Amalekites</hi> who plundered Ziklag; they were not many, but they were all mighty men and did David good service upon that occasion, <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.1-1Sam.30.31">1 Sam. xxx.</reference> See how Providence provides. David's interest grew strangely just when he had occasion to make use of it, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.22">v. 22</reference>. Auxiliary forces flocked in daily, <hi type="italic">till he had a great host.</hi> When the promise comes to the birth, leave it to God to find strength to bring forth.
entries.185a879d234ec5fd1db97c8a29dcbcd7a35a5fb0: <div eID="gen7761" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Army. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1048.)</title> <div sID="gen7762" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the numbers of the bands <hi type="italic">that were</hi> ready armed to the war, <hi type="italic">and</hi> came to David to Hebron, to turn the kingdom of Saul to him, according to the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">24</hi> The children of Judah that bare shield and spear <hi type="italic">were</hi> six thousand and eight hundred, ready armed to the war. <hi type="super">25</hi> Of the children of Simeon, mighty men of valour for the war, seven thousand and one hundred. <hi type="super">26</hi> Of the children of Levi four thousand and six hundred. <hi type="super">27</hi> And Jehoiada <hi type="italic">was</hi> the leader of the Aaronites, and with him <hi type="italic">were</hi> three thousand and seven hundred; <hi type="super">28</hi> And Zadok, a young man mighty of valour, and of his father's house twenty and two captains. <hi type="super">29</hi> And of the children of Benjamin, the kindred of Saul, three thousand: for hitherto the greatest part of them had kept the ward of the house of Saul. <hi type="super">30</hi> And of the children of Ephraim twenty thousand and eight hundred, mighty men of valour, famous throughout the house of their fathers. <hi type="super">31</hi> And of the half tribe of Manasseh eighteen thousand, which were expressed by name, to come and make David king. <hi type="super">32</hi> And of the children of Issachar, <hi type="italic">which were men</hi> that had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do; the heads of them <hi type="italic">were</hi> two hundred; and all their brethren <hi type="italic">were</hi> at their commandment. <hi type="super">33</hi> Of Zebulun, such as went forth to battle, expert in war, with all instruments of war, fifty thousand, which could keep rank: <hi type="italic">they were</hi> not of double heart. <hi type="super">34</hi> And of Naphtali a thousand captains, and with them with shield and spear thirty and seven thousand. <hi type="super">35</hi> And of the Danites expert in war twenty and eight thousand and six hundred. <hi type="super">36</hi> And of Asher, such as went forth to battle, expert in war, forty thousand. <hi type="super">37</hi> And on the other side of Jordan, of the Reubenites, and the Gadites, and of the half tribe of Manasseh, with all manner of instruments of war for the battle, a hundred and twenty thousand. <hi type="super">38</hi> All these men of war, that could keep rank, came with a perfect heart to Hebron, to make David king over all Israel: and all the rest also of Israel <hi type="italic">were</hi> of one heart to make David king. <hi type="super">39</hi> And there they were with David three days, eating and drinking: for their brethren had prepared for them. <hi type="super">40</hi> Moreover they that were nigh them, <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto Issachar and Zebulun and Naphtali, brought bread on asses, and on camels, and on mules, and on oxen, <hi type="italic">and</hi> meat, meal, cakes of figs, and bunches of raisins, and wine, and oil, and oxen, and sheep abundantly: for <hi type="italic">there was</hi> joy in Israel. <div eID="gen7762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7763" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of those who were active in perfecting the settlement of David upon the throne, after the death of Ishbosheth. We read (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.1">ch. xi. 1</reference>, and before <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.1">2 Sam. v. 1</reference>) that <hi type="italic">all the tribes of Israel came,</hi> either themselves or by their representatives, to Hebron, to make David king; now here we have an account of the quota which every tribe brought in <hi type="italic">ready armed to the war,</hi> in case there should be any opposition, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.23">v. 23</reference>. We may observe here, <div eID="gen7763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7764" type="x-p"/> I. That those tribes that lived nearest brought the fewest-Judah but 6800 (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.24">v. 24</reference>), Simeon but 7100 (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.25">v. 25</reference>); whereas Zebulun, that lay remote, brought 50,000, Asher 40,000, and the two tribes and a half on the other side Jordan 120 000. Not as if the next adjacent tribes were cold in the cause; but they showed as much of their prudence in bringing few, since all the rest lay so near within call, as the others did of their zeal in bringing so many. The men of Judah had enough to do to entertain those that came from afar. <div eID="gen7764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7765" type="x-p"/> II. The Levites themselves, and the priests (called here the <hi type="italic">Aaronites</hi>), appeared very hearty in this cause, and were ready, if there were occasion, to fight for David, as well as pray for him, because they knew he was called of God to the government, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.26-1Chr.12.28">v. 26-28</reference>. <div eID="gen7765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7766" type="x-p"/> III. Even some of the kindred of Saul came over to David (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.29">v. 29</reference>), not so many as of the other tribes, because a foolish affection for their own tribe, and a jealousy for the honour of it, kept many of them long in the sinking interest of Saul's family. Kindred should never over-rule conscience. Call no man <hi type="italic">Father</hi> to this extent, but God only. <div eID="gen7766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7767" type="x-p"/> IV. It is said of most of these that they were <hi type="italic">mighty men of valour</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.25">v. 25</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.28">28</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.30">30</reference>), of others that they were <hi type="italic">expert in war</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.35-1Chr.12.36">v. 35, 36</reference>), and of them all that they <hi type="italic">could keep rank,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.38">v. 38</reference>. They had a great deal of martial fire, and yet were governable and subject to the rules of order—warm hearts but cool heads. <div eID="gen7767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7768" type="x-p"/> V. Some were so considerate as to bring with them arms, and all instruments for war (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.24">v. 24</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.33">33</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.37">37</reference>), for how could they think that David should be able to furnish them? <div eID="gen7768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7769" type="x-p"/> VI. The men of Issachar were the fewest of all, only 200, and yet as serviceable to David's interest as those that brought in the greatest numbers, these few being in effect the whole tribe. For, 1. They were men of great skill above any of their neighbours, men that <hi type="italic">had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do.</hi> They understood the natural times, could <hi type="italic">discern the face of the sky,</hi> were weather-wise, could advise their neighbours in the proper times for ploughing, sowing reaping, &c. Or the ceremonial times, the times appointed for the solemn feasts; therefore they are said to <hi type="italic">call the people to the mountain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.19">Deut. xxxiii. 19</reference>), for almanacs were not then so common as now. Or, rather, the political times; they understood public affairs, the temper of the nation, and the tendencies of the present events. It is the periphrasis of statesmen that they <hi type="italic">know the times,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.1.13">Esth. i. 13</reference>. Those of that tribe were greatly intent on public affairs, had good intelligence from abroad and made a good use of it. They knew <hi type="italic">what Israel ought to do:</hi> from their observation and experience they learned both their own and others' duty and interest. In this critical juncture they knew Israel ought to make David king. It was not only expedient, but necessary; the present posture of affairs called for it. The men of Issachar dealt mostly in country business, and did not much intermeddle in public affairs, which gave them an opportunity of observing others and conversing with themselves. A stander-by sees sometimes more than a gamester. 2. They were men of great interests; for <hi type="italic">all their brethren were at their commandment.</hi> The commonality of that tribe having <hi type="italic">bowed their shoulder to bear</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.15">Gen. xlix. 15</reference>), the great men had them at their beck. Hence we read of <hi type="italic">the princes of Issachar,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.5.15">Judg. v. 15</reference>. They knew how to rule, and the rest knew how to obey. It is happy indeed when those that should lead are intelligent and judicious, and those who are to follow are modest and obsequious. <div eID="gen7769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7770" type="x-p"/> VII. It is said of them all that they engaged in this enterprise <hi type="italic">with a perfect heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.38">v. 38</reference>), and particularly of the men of Zebulun that they were <hi type="italic">not of double heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.33">v. 33</reference>. They were, in this matter, <hi type="italic">Israelites indeed, in whom was no guile.</hi> And this was their perfection, that they were of one heart, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.38">v. 38</reference>. None had any separate interests, but all for the public good. <div eID="gen7770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7771" type="x-p"/> VIII. The men of Judah, and others of the adjacent tribes, prepared for the victualling of their respective camps when they came to Hebron, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.39-1Chr.12.40">v. 39, 40</reference>. Those that were at the least pains in travelling to this convention, or congress of states, thought themselves obliged to be at so much the more charge in entertaining the rest, that there might be something of an equality. A noble feast was made (was <hi type="italic">made for laughter,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.19">Eccl. x. 19</reference>) upon this occasion, for there was <hi type="italic">joy in Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.40">v. 40</reference>. And good reason; for <hi type="italic">when the righteous</hi> bear <hi type="italic">rule the city rejoices.</hi> Thus, when the throne of Christ is set up in a soul, there is, or ought to be, great joy in that soul: and provision is made for the feasting of it, not as here for two or three days, but for the whole life, nay, for eternity.  <chapter eID="1Chr.12"/> <div eID="gen7771" type="x-p"/>

entries.70d40466aadd92d6f13c536d3f6a2b919e756f76: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3738"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 12</title> <div sID="gen5353" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.1-1Chr.12.22">1Ch 12:1-22</reference>. The Companies That Came to David at Ziklag.<div eID="gen5353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5354" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3738"/><hi type="bold">1-7. Now these are they that came to David to Ziklag--</hi>There are three lists given in this chapter, arranged, apparently, according to the order of time when the parties joined the standard of David.<div eID="gen5354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5355" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">while he yet kept himself close because of Saul--</hi>that is, when the king's jealousy had driven him into exile from the court and the country.<div eID="gen5355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5356" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ziklag--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.6">1Sa 27:6</reference>). It was during his retirement in that Philistine town that he was joined in rapid succession by the heroes who afterwards contributed so much to the glory of his reign. <div eID="gen5356" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f3b9256a519f99b349f132852bcc733bf1b76d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3741"/><div sID="gen5359" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3741"/><hi type="bold">8-13. of the Gadites there separated themselves unto David--</hi>that is, from the service of Saul and from the rest of the Gadites who remained steadfast adherents of his cause.<div eID="gen5359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5360" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into the hold--</hi>or fortress, that is, of Ziklag, which was in the wilderness of Judah.<div eID="gen5360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5361" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whose faces were like the faces of lions, &c.--</hi>A fierce, lion-like countenance (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.23">2Sa 1:23</reference>), and great agility in pursuit (<reference osisRef="2Sam.2.18">2Sa 2:18</reference>), were qualities of the highest estimation in ancient warfare. <div eID="gen5361" type="x-p"/>
entries.32a4a16a6643eb8eb05bff2a89184ea855fd6328: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3742"/><div sID="gen5362" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3742"/><hi type="bold">14. one of the least was over an hundred, and the greatest over a thousand--</hi>David, while at Ziklag, had not so large an amount of forces as to give to each of these the command of so many men. Another meaning, therefore, must obviously be sought, and excluding was, which is a supplement by our translators, the import of the passage is, that one of the least could discomfit a hundred, and the greatest was worth a thousand ordinary men; a strong hyperbole to express their uncommon valor. <div eID="gen5362" type="x-p"/>
entries.81042bf6d438365de9f917e6adb34383a1384846: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3743"/><div sID="gen5363" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3743"/><hi type="bold">15. These are they that went over Jordan in the first month--</hi>that is, in spring, when the swollen river generally fills up the banks of its channel (see on <reference osisRef="Josh.3.14">Jos 3:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.4.19">Jos 4:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.5.10">Jos 5:10</reference>).<div eID="gen5363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5364" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they put to flight all them of the valleys--</hi>This was probably done at the time of their separating themselves and their purpose being discovered, they had to cut their passage through the opposing adherents of Saul, both on the eastern and western banks. The impossibility of taking the fords at such a time, and the violent rapidity of the current, make this crossing of the Jordan--in whatever way these Gadites accomplished it--a remarkable feat. <div eID="gen5364" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ccdce5e0f91642538a374ee77a4c8132a491ec6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3744"/><div sID="gen5365" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3744"/><hi type="bold">16. the children of Benjamin and Judah--</hi>It is probable that the Benjamites invited the Judahites to accompany them, in order to prevent David being suspicious of them. Their anticipations, as the result showed, were well founded. He did suspect them, but the doubts of David as to their object in repairing to him, were promptly dispelled by Amasai or Amasa, who, by the secret impulse of the Spirit, assured him of their strong attachment and their zealous service from a unanimous conviction that his cause was owned and blessed of God (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.12-1Sam.18.14">1Sa 18:12-14</reference>). <div eID="gen5365" type="x-p"/>
entries.947091295d31a2c19fef115a2a3c737d3d2e8d14: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3745"/><div sID="gen5366" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3745"/><hi type="bold">19-22. there fell some of Manasseh--</hi>The period of their accession is fixed as the time when David came with the Philistines against Saul to battle.<div eID="gen5366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5367" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but they helped them not--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.4">1Sa 29:4</reference>). <div eID="gen5367" type="x-p"/>
entries.a1153ad32519df9f9624c23767daeab7887f7b32: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3749"/><div sID="gen5373" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3749"/><hi type="bold">23. these are the numbers of the bands ... that came to David to Hebron--</hi>after the death of Ish-bosheth (see on <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.1">2Sa 5:1</reference>).<div eID="gen5373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5374" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to turn the kingdom of Saul to him, according to the word of the Lord--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Chr.10.14">1Ch 10:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.3">11:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.10">10</reference>). The account commences with the southern tribes, Levi being associated with Judah and Simeon, as the great majority of the leading men in this tribe resided in Judah; and, after recounting the representatives of the northern tribes, it concludes with those on the east of Jordan. <div eID="gen5374" type="x-p"/>
entries.89af4f9d1f6d943f70ab1b53ce48c557eb488424: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3750"/><div sID="gen5375" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3750"/><hi type="bold">27. Jehoiada, the leader of the Aaronites--</hi>not the high priest, for that was Abiathar (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.9">1Sa 23:9</reference>), but the leader of the Aaronite warriors, supposed to be the father of Benaiah (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.22">1Ch 11:22</reference>). <div eID="gen5375" type="x-p"/>
entries.a145335e98c5a326b659e646568ac5956fa64197: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3751"/><div sID="gen5376" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3751"/><hi type="bold">29. Benjamin ... three thousand--</hi>This small number shows the unpopularity of the movement in this tribe; and, indeed, it is expressly stated that the mass of the population had, even after Ish-bosheth's death, anxiously endeavored to secure the crown in the family of Saul. <div eID="gen5376" type="x-p"/>
entries.1162d28f02feaf1b2e102200046f4d0e25135c0e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3752"/><div sID="gen5377" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3752"/><hi type="bold">32. children of Issachar, ... that had understanding of the times, &c.--</hi>Jewish writers say that the people of this tribe were eminent for their acquirements in astronomical and physical science; and the object of the remark was probably to show that the intelligent and learned classes were united with the military, and had declared for David. <div eID="gen5377" type="x-p"/>
entries.ec4cfddbaaf93d09c13718a027ac408297735c69: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3753"/><div sID="gen5378" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3753"/><hi type="bold">33. Zebulun ... could keep rank--</hi>that is, were more disciplined soldiers than the rest.<div eID="gen5378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5379" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not of double heart--</hi>Though their numbers were large, all were in a high degree well affected to David. <div eID="gen5379" type="x-p"/>
entries.e888a2e18b1a3ed9809ccb9c4bea9afacbe19ac1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3754"/><div sID="gen5380" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3754"/><hi type="bold">38. all the rest also of Israel were of one heart to make David king--</hi>that is, entertained a unanimous desire for his elevation. <div eID="gen5380" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f9552404515a5e0e7976e6afe62dc470956f5e5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3755"/><div sID="gen5381" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3755"/><hi type="bold">39-40. there they were with David three days, eating and drinking--</hi>According to the statements made in the preceding verses, the number of armed warriors assembled in Hebron on this occasion amounted to three hundred thousand. Supplies of provisions were abundantly furnished, not only by the people of the neighborhood, but from distant parts of the country, for all wished the festivities to be on a scale of liberality and magnificence suitable to the auspicious occasion. <chapter eID="1Chr.12"/>

entries.36000f65802fe2265b4dbdad9abe9a30d5a350f7: <div eID="gen13586" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen13587" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13588" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13588" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13587" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13589" type="x-p"/> The different persons, captains, etc., who joined themselves to David at Ziklag, vv. 1-22. Those who joined him at Hebron, out of the different tribes; Judah, Simeon, Levi, the house of Aaron, Benjamin, Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, Zebulun, Naphtali, Dan, Asher, Reuben, etc., to the amount of a hundred and twenty thousand, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.23-1Chr.12.37">1Chr 12:23-37</reference>. Their unanimity, and the provisions they brought for his support, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.38-1Chr.12.40">1Chr 12:38-40</reference>. <div eID="gen13589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13590" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen13590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13591" type="x-p"/> Came to David to Ziklag - Achish, king of Gath, had given Ziklag to David, as a safe retreat from the wrath of Saul.
entries.f768d9ad8dd8bd0c9409ebeb9fb7251e4a053405: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen13591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13592" type="x-p"/> And were as swift as the roes - That swiftness was considered to be a grand accomplishment in a warrior, appears from all ancient writings which treat of military affairs.
entries.dfd31a2cf3041d546d92732f769c51a39ca4d666: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen13592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13593" type="x-p"/> In the first month - Perhaps this was the month Nisan, which answers to a part of our March and April. This was probably before the snows on the mountains were melted, just as Jordan began to overflow its banks; or if we allow that it had already overflowed its banks, it made their attempt more hazardous, and afforded additional proof of their heroism.
entries.9d11b026d91a4537ff2db70161cf5cdbf7c9f9e4: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen13593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13594" type="x-p"/> The spirit came upon Amasai - "The spirit of fortitude clothed Amasai, the chief of the mighty men; and he answered, For thy sake, O David, are we come, that we may be with thee, thou son of Jesse. <div eID="gen13594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13595" type="x-p"/> Prosperity be to thee by night and by day; and prosperity be to thy helpers; for the Word of the Lord is thy assistant." - T.
entries.02c4848175acd594c00fe621375db34c847a997f: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen13595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13596" type="x-p"/> Like the host of God - "That is, a very numerous army; like the army of the angel of God." - T.
entries.4fbe1609e27504f65aae515d3cf500aa926dc318: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen13596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13597" type="x-p"/> And came to David to Hebron - That is, after the death of Ish-bosheth, Saul's son. See <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.5">2Sam 4:5</reference>.
entries.ee54f8a79589981e0a85c4cb00f8e4b8450fb7c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen13597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13598" type="x-p"/> Jehoiada was the leader of the Aaronites - Abiathar was then high priest, and Jehoiada captain over the warriors of the house of Aaron.
entries.e9276695f6daa563c35b9aa794348e05ef131237: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen13598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13599" type="x-p"/> Children of Issachar - According to the Targum they were all astronomers and astrologers: "and the sons of Issachar, who had understanding to know the times, and were skilled in fixing the beginnings of years, the commencement of months, and the intercalation of months and years; skillful in the changes of the moon, and in fixing the lunar solemnities to their proper times; skillful also in the doctrine of the solar periods; astrologers in signs and stars, that they might show Israel what to do; and their teachers were two hundred chiefs of the Sanhedrin: and all their brethren excelled in the words of the law, and were endued with wisdom, and were obedient to their command." - T. It appears that in their wisdom, experience, and skill, their brethren had the fullest confidence; and nothing was done but by their direction and advice.
entries.8dc9cad5c1e268fa6b4870376f226edcd97177ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen13599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13600" type="x-p"/> They were with David three days - These were the deputies of the different people mentioned here: it is not possible that all the thousands mentioned above could have feasted with David for three days; and yet it appears there was even of these a great number, for the men of Issachar, Zebulun, and Naphtali, who were nearest to this place of rendezvous, had brought all the necessaries for such a feast. From the whole it appears most evident that the great majority of the tribes of Israel wished to see the kingdom confirmed in the hands of David; nor was there ever in any country a man more worthy of the public choice. As a statesman, warrior, hero, poet, and divine, he stands unrivalled in the annals of the world: by him alone were the Israelites raised to a pitch of the highest splendor; and their name became a terror to their enemies, and a praise in the earth. But, alas, how are the mighty now fallen!  <chapter eID="1Chr.12"/> <div eID="gen13600" type="x-p"/>

entries.c1b7bb2f11fd4fee449ad018545ccf9d6bbba9de: <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.1">1Ch 12:1</reference> <hi type="italic">The Benjamites who came to David to Ziklag.</hi> - 1Ch 12:1. Ziklag was originally allotted to the Simeonites by Joshua (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.5">Jos 19:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.30">1Ch 4:30</reference>), but at a later time came into possession of the Philistines, and was assigned and presented by king Achish to David, who had fled for refuge to him, as a dwelling-place for himself and his followers; see <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.1">1Sa 27:1</reference>-7. As to its situation, which has not yet been with certainty ascertained, see the discussion on Jos 15:31. In it David dwelt for a year and four months, until he went to Hebron on the death of Saul. During this time it was that the warriors of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned in the succeeding register went over to him, as we learn from the words עצוּר עוד, “he was still held back before Saul,” a concise expression for “while he was still held back before Saul.” This last expression, however, does not signify, “hindered from coming before Saul” (Berth.), but <hi type="italic">inter Israelitas publice versari prohibitus</hi> (J. H. Mich.), or rather, “before Saul, imprisoned as it were, without being able to appear in a manner corresponding to his divine election to be ruler over Israel.” בגב והמּה, and they were among the heroes, i.e., belonged to the heroes, the helpers of the war, i.e., to those who helped him in his former wars; cf. 1Ch 12:17., 21f.
entries.70b0b80207d6cb9df5871b1d15cc450423b4c0ba: <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.2-1Chr.12.4">1Ch 12:2-4</reference> קשׁת נשׁקי, “those preparing bows,” i.e., those armed with bows, synonymous with קשׁת דּרכי   (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.40">1Ch 8:40</reference>); cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.17">2Ch 17:17</reference>; Psa 78:9. “With the right and left hand practised upon stones,” i.e., to hurl stones, cf. Jdg 20:16; “and in arrows on the bow,” i.e., to shoot therewith. שׁאוּל מאחי, of Saul’s brethren, i.e., of the men of the tribe, not “of his nearer relatives,” and consequently of Benjamin, has been added as an explanation; cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.29">1Ch 12:29</reference>, where בנימן בּני and שׁאוּל אחי are synonyms. - In 1Ch 12:3. we have the names. הראשׁ, the head, i.e., the leader of this host of warriors; compare <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.7">1Ch 5:7</reference>, 1Ch 5:12. הגּבעתי, cf. Gibeah of Saul or Benjamin, cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.31">1Ch 11:31</reference>; and for its situation, see on Jos 18:28. הענתתי, from the priests’ city Anathoth, now Anata; see on Jos 18:24. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.4">1Ch 12:4</reference> the Gibeonite Ismaiah is called “hero among the thirty, and over the thirty,” - words which can hardly have any other sense than that Ismaiah belonged also to David’s corps of thirty heroes (1 Chron 11), and was (temporarily) their leader, although his name does not occur in 1 Chron 11. It is probable that the reason of the omission was, that at the time when the list was prepared he was no longer alive. הגּדרתי, of Gedera, a city of the tribe of Judah in the <hi type="italic">Shephelah</hi>, which, according to Van de Velde (<hi type="italic">Reise,</hi> ii. S. 166), was probably identical with the village Ghedera, which lies to the left of the road Tel-es-Safieh to Akir, about an hour to the south-west of Jabne. In any case, it corresponds well with the statements of the <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi> As to Gedrus, or Gaedur, see on Jos 15:36. Immediately afterwards in <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.7">1Ch 12:7</reference> Gedor is mentioned, a city in the mountains of Judah, to the westward of the road which leads from Hebron to Jerusalem (see on <reference osisRef="Josh.15.58">Jos 15:58</reference>); and from that fact Bertheau imagines we must conclude that the men of Judah are enumerated as well as the Benjamites. But this conclusion is not valid; for from the very beginning, when the domains and cities were assigned to the individual tribes under Joshua, they were not the exclusive possession of the individual tribes, and at a later period they were still less so. In course of time the respective tribal domains underwent (in consequence of wars and other events) many alterations, not only in extent, but also in regard to their inhabitants, so that in Saul’s time single Benjamite families may quite well have had their home in the cities of Judah.
entries.a186265cc2b57c04758e88a33a43f39ec8d74528: <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.5-1Chr.12.7">1Ch 12:5-7</reference> החרוּפי (<hi type="italic">Keri</hi> החריפי) is a patronymic, which denotes either one descended from Haruph, or belonging to the חריף בּני mentioned in <reference osisRef="Neh.7.34">Neh 7:34</reference> along with the Gibeonites. The קרחים, Korahites, in <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.6">1Ch 12:6</reference> are, without doubt (cf. Delitzsch,<hi type="italic">Ps</hi>. S. 300), descendants of the Levite Korah, one division of whom David made guardian of the thresholds of the tent erected for the ark of the covenant on Zion, because their fathers had been watchers of the entrance of the camp of Jahve, i.e., had in that earlier time held the office of watchers by the tabernacle; see on 1Ch 9:18. The names Elkanah and Azareel are thoroughly Levitic names, and their service in the porter’s office in the holy place may have roused in them the desire to fight for David, the chosen of the Lord. But there is no reason why we should, with Bertheau, interpret the words as denoting descendants of the almost unknown Korah of the tribe of Judah (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.43">1Ch 2:43</reference>), or, with the older commentators, refer it to some other unmentioned Benjamite who bore this name. The explanation of the connection existing between these Levitic Korahites and the Benjamites, which is presupposed by the mention of them among the Benjamites, may be found in the fact that the Levites received no tribal domain of their own, and possessed only cities for dwelling in in the domains of the other tribes, with whom they were consequently civilly incorporated, so that those who dwelt in the cities of Benjamin were properly reckoned among the Benjamites. At the partition of the land under Joshua, it is true, only the priests received their cities in Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin; while, on the contrary, the Kohathites, who were not priests, among whom the Korahites were, received their cities in the tribal domain of Ephraim, Dan, and half-Manasseh (Josh 21:9-26). But when the tabernacle was transferred from Shiloh to Nob, and afterwards to Gibeon, the Korahite doorkeepers must, without doubt, have migrated to one of the Levitic cities of Benjamin, probably for the most part to Gibeon, and who were reckoned among the Benjamites. As to הגּדור מן,<hi type="italic">vide </hi> 1Ch 12:4. If this be so, there remains no cogent reason for supposing that in our register, besides the Benjamites, men out of other tribes are also introduced. With that there falls away at once Bertheau’s further conclusion, that the author of the Chronicle has considerably abridged the register, and that from <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Chr.12.4">1Ch 12:4</reference></hi> onwards men of Judah also are named, the list of whom must certainly (?) have been originally introduced by special superscription similar to those in <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.8">1Ch 12:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.16">1Ch 12:16</reference>, 1Ch 12:19. His further reason for his conjecture - namely, that our register makes use of the qualificative epithets, “the Gibeathite,” “the Anathothite,” etc., only in a few special cases-is of no force whatever; for we are not justified in assuming that we may expect to find here, as in the register in 1 Chron 11:26-47, such qualificatives after every individual name. The character of our register cannot be arrived at by a comparison with the list of David’s heroes in 1 Chron 11; it should rather be sought for by comparing it with the succeeding list, whose contents are of a similar kind with its own. David’s chosen corps of thirty heroes was much more important for the history of his reign, than the lists of the men who joined themselves to him and fought on his behalf before he ascended the throne. For that reason the thirty heroes are not only mentioned by name, but their descent also is told us, while that more detailed information is not given with regard to the others just mentioned. Only the names of the Gadites and Manassites are mentioned; of the Benjamites and men of Judah, who came to him in the mountain fastness (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.16-1Chr.12.18">1Ch 12:16-18</reference>), the name of only one, Amasai, is given; while of the Benjamites who came to Ziklag, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.3-1Chr.12.7">1Ch 12:3-7</reference>, such qualificative statements are made in reference to only a few individuals, and in these cases the object probably was to distinguish them from other well-known persons of the same name.
entries.36dedffa348eeb355ba2e93e4efc95959ab93658: <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.8-1Chr.12.13">1Ch 12:8-13</reference> <hi type="italic">The Gadites, Benjamites, and men of Judah who joined themselves to David during his sojourn in the mountain fastness.</hi> - 1Ch 12:8. David’s sojourn in the mountain hold falls in the first years of his flight from Saul, 1Sa 22:1. מצד, pointed with Pathach instead of with Kamets (מצד, cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.16">1Ch 12:16</reference>), on account of its intimate connection with מדבּרה, is synonymous with מצוּדה   (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.22">1Sa 24:22</reference>, etc.). The addition מדבּרה, “towards the wilderness,” shows that מצד denotes a mountain-top or mountain-fortress in the wilderness of Judah. If we compare the account in 1 Sam 22-24, we learn that David at that time did not hide himself in one single definite mountain-fortress, but sought and found resting-places, now here, now there, in the wilderness, on the summits of the hills (cf. בּמּצדות בּמּדבּר,   <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.14">1Sa 23:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.1">1Sa 24:1</reference>); so that מצד here is to be understood, as המּצוּדה,   <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.3">1Sa 24:3</reference>, also is, generally of the fastnesses in the mountains of Judah. At that time there gathered round David a great company of discontented and oppressed men, to the number of about 400, - men dissatisfied with Saul’s rule, whose leader he became, and who soon amounted to 600 men (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.2">1Sa 22:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.13">1Sa 23:13</reference>). To these belong the Gadites, and the men out of Benjamin and Judah, whose adhesion to David is noticed in our verses. נבדּלוּ, they separated themselves from the other Gadites who were on Saul’s side, “strong heroes,” as in <reference osisRef="Josh.8.3">Jos 8:3</reference>; cf. חיל גּבּורי, <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.24">1Ch 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.7.2">1Ch 7:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.7.9">1Ch 7:9</reference>, etc. למּלחמה צבא אנשׁי, men for service in the host for the war, i.e., combatants practised in war. ורמח צנּה ערכי, preparing shield and spear, i.e., wielding shield and spear, practised in their use: the preparing of these weapons includes the handling of them. Instead of ורמח, Veneta and many of the older copies have וּמגן; but it is not supported by MS authority, and moreover is not congruous with the passage. Lions’ faces their faces, i.e., lion-like in appearance, thoroughly warlike figures; cf. 2Sa 1:23. “As roes running swiftly on the mountains;” cf. 2Sa 2:18. This description of the strength and swiftness of these warriors recalls, as Bertheau remarks, the similar expressions used in the historical books concerning heroes of David’s time. It has manifestly been drawn from the original documents, not added by the chronicler. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.9-1Chr.12.13">1Ch 12:9-13</reference> the names are enumerated individually. עשׂר עשׁתּי, at the end of a series of ordinal numbers, denotes the eleventh; cf. 1Ch 24:12.
entries.c7b28e9561ad329582508881d0ee06fd8222d0f0: <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.14-1Chr.12.15">1Ch 12:14-15</reference> הצּבא ראשׁי, heads of the war-host, i.e., chief warriors, not leaders of the host. וגו למאה אחד, “one for a hundred, (viz.) the small and the greater for a thousand,” i.e., the smaller (weaker) could cope with a hundred, the stronger with a thousand men; cf. Lev 26:8. This, which is the only correct interpretation, is that received by Bertheau and the older Jewish commentators. The Vulgate, on the contrary, translates, <hi type="italic">novissimus centum militibus praeerat et maximus mille</hi>, which is inadmissible, for in that case על must have been used instead of ל. The אחד belongs to both the clauses which it precedes, to הקּטן and to הגּדול, and is placed immediately before למאה to emphasize the contrast between one and a hundred. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.15">1Ch 12:15</reference> we have a proof of their valour, in an account of a bold exploit performed by them. In the first month of the year, that is, in spring, when the Jordan overflows all its banks, they crossed the river and put to flight all the dwellers in the valleys towards the east and towards the west. This happened, probably, when they separated themselves from their brethren and went over to David, when they must have had to cut their way through the adherents of Saul (Berth.). The Piel מלּא with על denotes to make full, to make to run over, in the signification to overflow. The Kethibh גּדיתיו comes from גּדיה elsewhere only the plural גּדתיו, so also here in the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>. In the dry summer season the Jordan may be crossed by wading at various points (fords); while in spring, on the contrary, when it is so swollen by the melting snows of Lebanon, that in some parts it overflows its banks, it is very dangerous to attempt to cross. See on Jos 3:15. העמקים, “the valleys,” for the inhabitants of the valleys.
entries.a0ab8250c7a5b9a262202c5543b0d031a2c59616: <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.16-1Chr.12.17">1Ch 12:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen5696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5697" type="x-p"/> There came to David in the mountain-fastness also men of Benjamin and Judah (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.8">1Ch 12:8</reference>). Their names are not in the lists, possibly because they were not handed down in the historical works made use of by the chronicler. At their head, as we learn from <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.18">1Ch 12:18</reference>, stood Amasai, chief of the thirty, i.e., of the corps formed of the thirty heroes (see <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.11">1Ch 11:11</reference>), although his name does not occur in the catalogue, 1 Chron 11. According to this, Amasai must have occupied a very important position under David; but since the name עמשׂי is not elsewhere mentioned in the history of David, the older commentators have conjectured that עמשׂי may have been the same person as עמשׂא, son of Abigail (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.17">1Ch 2:17</reference>), whom Absalom made captain in Joab’s place, and whom David, after the victory over the rebels, wished to make commander-in-chief in the room of Joab, and whom for that reason Joab afterwards murdered (<reference osisRef="2Sam.17.25">2Sa 17:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.14">2Sa 19:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.4">2Sa 20:4</reference>, 2Sa 20:8.); or identical with אבשׁי the son of Zeruiah, <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.16">1Ch 2:16</reference> and 1Ch 11:20. Of these conjectures the first is much more probable than the second. To meet these men, David went forth from his fastness, and asked them with what purpose they came to him. “If for peace,” to stand by him, “then shall there be to me towards you a heart for union,” i.e., I will be with you of one heart, be true to you. ליחד לבב is plainer than אחד לב, 1Ch 12:38. “But if לרמּותני, to practise deceit against me (to be guilty of a מרמה) for mine enemies (to deliver me to them), although there be no wrong in my hands, the God of our fathers look thereon and punish;” cf. 2Ch 24:22. The God of our fathers, i.e., of the patriarchs (cf. Ezr 7:27; <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.6">2Ch 20:6</reference>, and Exo 3:13.), who rules in and over Israel, who shields the innocent and punishes the guilty.
entries.2ca8d6266d273a23085292c2f9f70422bf8c51f0: <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.18">1Ch 12:18</reference> <div eID="gen5697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5698" type="x-p"/> Then came the Spirit upon Amasai, so that he proclaimed himself enthusiastic for David and his cause. With לבשׁה רוּח cf. Jdg 6:34. Usually יהוה or אלהים is found with this expression (<reference osisRef="2Chr.24.20">2Ch 24:20</reference>), and here also the Spirit of God is meant; and אלהים is omitted only because all that was of importance here was to show that the resolution announced by Amasai was an effect of higher spiritual influence. לך, to thee, David (do we belong), thine are we. עמּך, “with thee,” sc. will we remain and fight. “Peace be to thee, and peace be to thy helpers; for thy God helpeth thee.” עזרך, He has helped thee in the fortunate combats in which you have heretofore been engaged (1Sa 18:12.), and He will help still further. David thereupon received them and made them captains of his band. הגּדוּד, the warrior-band, which had gathered round David, and were still gathering round him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.2">1Sa 22:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.8">1Sa 27:8</reference>, cf. also <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.21">1Ch 12:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.8">1Sa 30:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.15">1Sa 30:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.23">1Sa 30:23</reference>, etc.
entries.96fd04850b959d0927cfeaefb59327ca4316c564: <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.19-1Chr.12.20">1Ch 12:19-20</reference> <hi type="italic">The Manassites who went over to David before the last battle of the Philistines against Saul.</hi> - על גפל, to fall to one, is used specially of deserters in war who desert their lord and go over to the enemy: cf. 2Ki 25:11; 1Sa 29:3. אל יפּול, in the last clause of the verse, is a synonymous expression. The Manassites went over “when David went with the Philistines against Israel to the war, and (yet) helped them not; for upon advisement (בּעצה, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.20.18">Pro 20:18</reference>), the lords of the Philistines had sent him away, saying, 'For our heads, he will fall away to his master Saul.' “ <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.2-1Sam.29.11">1Sa 29:2-11</reference> contains the historical commentary on this event. When the lords of the Philistines collected their forces to march against Saul, David, who had found refuge with King Achish, was compelled to join the host of that prince with his band. But when the other Philistine princes saw the Hebrews, they demanded that they should be sent out of the army, as they feared that David might turn upon them during the battle, and so win favour by his treachery with Saul his lord. See the commentary on <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.1">1Sa 29:1</reference>-11. בּראשׁנוּ, for our heads, i.e., for the price of them, giving them as a price to obtain a friendly reception from Saul (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.4">1Sa 29:4</reference>). In consequence of this remonstrance, Achish requested David to return with his warriors to Ziklag. On this return march (“as he went to Ziklag,” cf. with בּלכתּו the ללכת of <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.11">1Sa 29:11</reference>), and consequently before the battle in which Saul lost his life (Berth.), and not after Saul’s great misfortune, as Ewald thinks, the Manassites whose names follow went over to David. The seven named in <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.20">1Ch 12:20</reference> were “heads of the thousands of Manasseh,” i.e., of the great families into which the tribe of Manasseh was divided, and as such were leaders of the Manassite forces in war: cf. Num 31:14 with <reference osisRef="Exod.18.25">Exo 18:25</reference>, and the commentary on the latter passage.
entries.e7f9551da77f6b1f97fed2aa19c9507ff225413d: <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.21">1Ch 12:21</reference> <div eID="gen5698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5699" type="x-p"/> These<note placement="foot">We take והמּה to refer to the Manassites named in <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.20">1Ch 12:20</reference>, like the והמּה of <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.1">1Ch 12:1</reference> and the הם אלּה הם eht of 1Ch 12:15. Bertheau, on the contrary, thinks on various grounds that המּה refers to all the heroes who have been spoken of in vv. 1-20. In the first place, it was not the Manassites alone who took part in the conflict with Amalek, for David won the victory with his whole force of 600 men (<reference osisRef="1Sam.30.9">1Sa 30:9</reference>), among whom, without doubt, those named in vv. 1-18 were included. Then, secondly, a clear distinction is made between those who gave in their adhesion to and helped David at an earlier period (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.1">1Ch 12:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.7">1Ch 12:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.22">1Ch 12:22</reference>), and those who came to him in Hebron (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.23">1Ch 12:23</reference>). And finally, the general remark in <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.22">1Ch 12:22</reference> is connected with <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.21">1Ch 12:21</reference> by the grounding כּי, so that we must regard <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.21">1Ch 12:21</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.22">1Ch 12:22</reference> as a subscription closing the preceding catalogues. but none of these arguments are very effective. The grounding כי in <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.22">1Ch 12:22</reference> does not refer to the whole of <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.21">1Ch 12:21</reference>, but only to the last clause, or, to be more accurate, only to בּצּבא, showing that David had an army. The second proves nothing, and in the first only so much is correct, that not merely the seven Manassites named in <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.20">1Ch 12:20</reference> took, part in the battle with Amalek, but also the warriors who had formerly gone over to David; but from that there is not the slightest reason to conclude that this is expressed by והמּה. It is manifest from the context and the plan of the register, that וגו עזרוּ והמּה can only refer to those of whom it is said in <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.20">1Ch 12:20</reference> that they went over to David as he was returning to Ziklag. If <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.21">1Ch 12:21</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.22">1Ch 12:22</reference> were a subscription to all the preceding registers, instead of והמּה another expression which would separate the verse somewhat more from that immediately preceding would have been employed, perhaps כּל־אלה.</note> helped David הגּדוּד על, against the detachment of Amalekites, who during David’s absence had surprised and burnt Ziklag, and led captive the women and children (<reference osisRef="1Sam.30.1-1Sam.30.10">1Sa 30:1-10</reference>). This interpretation, which Rashi also has (<hi type="italic">contra turmam Amalekitarum</hi>), and which the Vulgate hints at in its <hi type="italic">adversus latrunculos</hi>, rests upon the fact that in <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.8">1Sa 30:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.15">1Sa 30:15</reference>, the word הגּדוּד, which in general only denotes single detachments or predatory bands, is used of the Amalekite band; whence the word can only refer to the march of David against the Amalekites, of which we have an account in 1Sa 30:9., and not to the combats which he had with Saul. “For they were all valiant heroes, and were שׂרים, captains in the army,” sc. which gathered round David.
entries.beb1dc8a0fcc6f0819ce51a3734d306d196511a3: <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.22">1Ch 12:22</reference> “For every day” (בּיום יום לעת, at the time of each day) “came (people) to David to help him, until to a great host, like a host of God,” i.e., until his band grew to a camp like to a host of God. אלהים מחנה, a host which God has formed, and in which the power of God shows itself; cf. hills and cedars of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.36.7">Psa 36:7</reference>; Psa 80:11. In these concluding remarks to the enumeration by name of the valiant men who during Saul’s lifetime went over to David, there is no exaggeration which would betray an idealizing historian (Movers, S. 270). The greatness of a host of God is to be estimated according to the power and the spirit, not according to the number, of the warriors, so that we need not take the words to mean a host of thousands and tens of thousands. David had at first 400, afterwards 600, valiant warriors, against whom Saul with his thousands could accomplish nothing. The increase in their number from 400 to 600 shows that the host increased from day to day, especially when we keep in mind the fact that after Saul’s defeat considerable bands of fugitives must certainly have gone over to David before he was anointed in Hebron to be king over Judah. The expression is only rhetorical, not idealizing or exaggerating.
entries.3d56df8d09fb8e7018659124095b50aefcceb847: <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.23-1Chr.12.40">1Ch 12:23-40</reference> <hi type="italic">List of the warriors who made David king in Hebron.</hi> - The superscription (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.23">1Ch 12:23</reference>) runs: “These are the numbers of the bands of the men equipped for war, who came,” etc. החלוּץ is a collective noun, denoting the equipped manhood. ראשׁי signifies here, not <hi type="italic">principes exercitus</hi>, as the Vulgate renders it, heads, i.e., leaders of the army (Berth.), but literally denotes sums, i.e., companies, bands of soldiers, as in Jdg 7:16, Jdg 7:20; Jdg 9:34, Jdg 9:37, Jdg 9:44; <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.1">1Sa 11:1</reference>; or it may perhaps also be heads for individuals, as ראשׁ in Jdg 5:30. Both these meanings are linguistically certain; so that we cannot say, with Bertheau, that ראשׁי before החלוּץ denotes, according to the well-ascertained use of language, leaders of the army, and that גלגלת would have been used had it been wished to express the number by heads, e.g., 1 Chron 23:3-24. That use of the word is indeed also found, but it cannot be proved to be the only proper one. If we take ראשׁי here to denote leaders, we bring the superscription into irreconcilable contradiction with the contents of the following catalogue, which gives the names of the heads and the number of the warriors (1Ch 12:27.) only in the case of the families of Aaron, and in that of Issachar the number of the princes; while in the case of the other tribes we have only the numbers of the bands or detachments. This contradiction cannot be got rid of, as Bertheau imagines, by the hypothesis that the superscription referred originally to a catalogue which was throughout similar in plan to that which we find in <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.26-1Chr.12.28">1Ch 12:26-28</reference>, and that the author of the Chronicle has very considerably abridged the more detailed statements of the original documents which he used. This hypothesis is a mere makeshift, in which we have the less need “to take refuge,” as the catalogue has neither the appearance of having been abridged or revised by the author of our Chronicle. It is shown to be a faithful copy of a more ancient authority, both by the characteristic remarks which it contains on the individual tribes, and by the inequality in the numbers. Bertheau, indeed, derives support for his hypothesis “from the inequality of the statements of number, and their relation to each other,” and upon that ground throws doubt upon the accuracy and correctness of the numbers, but in both cases without sufficient warrant. If we place the respective statements together synoptically, we see that there came to David to Hebron - <div eID="gen5699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5700" type="x-p"/> Of the tribe of: Judah 6,800 Of the tribe of: Ephraim 20,800 men <div eID="gen5706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5707" type="x-p"/> Of the half-tribe of: Manasseh 18,000 men <div eID="gen5707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5708" eID="gen5711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5712" type="x-p"/> Of the tribe of: Asher 40,000 men <div eID="gen5712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5713" type="x-p"/> Of two and a half trans-Jordanic tribes 120,000 men <div eID="gen5713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5714" type="x-p"/> Total 336,600 men with 1222 heads and captains <div eID="gen5714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5715" type="x-p"/> The total is not objected to by Bertheau, and its correctness is placed beyond a doubt by the recollection that we have here to do not with the representation of the various estates of the kingdom, but with a declaration of the will of the whole nation, who wished to make David their king. We must, if we are to estimate these statements, endeavour to go back in imagination to the circumstances of that time when Israel, although settled in the land, had not quite laid aside the character of a nation of warriors, in which every man capable of bearing arms marched to battle with, and for, his king. Now if the total number of fighting men in Israel was 600,000 in the time of Moses, and if, when the people were numbered in the last year of David’s reign, there were in Israel 800,000, and in Judah 500,000 (<reference osisRef="2Sam.24.9">2Sa 24:9</reference>), - the Levites being excluded in both cases - the 340,000 men of all the tribes, except Issachar, in reference to which no number is given, or after subtracting Judah and Levi, the 324,500 men out of the remaining tribes, is not much more than a half of the men capable of bearing arms in Moses’ time, and about a fourth part of the fighting population towards the end of David’s reign. But the relation of the numbers in the respective tribes, on the contrary, is somewhat surprising, and calls forth from Bertheau the following remarks: “To Judah, David’s tribe, which from the earliest time had been famous for its numbers and its powers, 6800 are assigned; to Zebulun, on the contrary, 50,000; to Naphtali, 1000 princes at the head of 37,000 warriors; to the two and a half East-Jordanic tribes, 120,000 men, etc. How does it happen that Zebulun and Naphtali, for example, two tribes that play no great part in Israel’s history, are so strongly represented, while Judah sends only a relatively small number of warriors?” To this question we answer, that Judah’s being represented by a number of warriors relatively so small, is accounted for simply by the fact that David had already been king over Judah for seven years, and consequently that tribe did not need to make him king by coming with the whole of its warriors, or the majority of them, when the other tribes were doing homage to David, but sent only a small number of its male population to this solemn act, who were witnesses in the name of the whole tribe to the homage proffered by the others. The same remark applies to the tribe of Simeon, whose domain was enclosed by that of Judah, and which had consequently recognised David as king at the same time as the larger tribe. In regard to the numbers of the other tribes, Levi had in the last year of David’s reign 38,000 men from thirty years old and upwards (<reference osisRef="1Chr.23.3">1Ch 23:3</reference>); and when here only 4600 Levites, besides the priestly families, are spoken of, the question arises, whether this number is to be understood to refer to the Levites in all the tribes, or only to those dwelling outside of Judah and Simeon, in the cities assigned to them by Moses and Joshua. The smallness of the number (3000) from the tribe of Benjamin is explained by the remark that the majority of this tribe still held to the house of Saul (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.29">1Ch 12:29</reference>). The only thing which is at all remarkable about the other numbers is, that the Ephraimites are so few (20,800 men) in contrast to the 180,000 men brought into the field by the half-tribe of Manasseh. But if we consider that Ephraim, which at the first census under Moses at Sinai had 40,500 men, had decreased to 32,500 at the second census in the wilderness of Moab, it is not improbable that at the time now treated of that tribe may not have been very strong in fighting men. For in Saul’s last war with the Philistines, when they had pressed forward so far as Mount Gilboa, and also in Abner’s struggle on behalf of King Ishbosheth for the re-conquest of the territory occupied by them, it probably suffered more, and was more weakened, than any of the other tribes. Perhaps also we may add that Ephraim, owing to its jealousy of Judah, which dates from the time of the judges, was not very much disposed to make David king over all Israel. That Zebulun and Naphtali are here so numerously represented, although they do not otherwise play an important part, is no reason for suspecting that the numbers given are incorrect. Since Zebulun under Moses numbered 57,400 men, and at a later time 60,500, and Naphtali 53,400 and 45,400 men capable of bearing arms respectively on the same occasions (see t. i. 2, S. 192); the first named tribe may easily have sent 50,000, the other 37,000 men to David, as the tribes dwelling in the north had been least affected by the wars which Israel carried on in the second half of the period of the judges and under Saul. Both of these tribes, too, are praised in the song of Deborah as a people ready to risk their lives for their fatherland (Jdg 5:18), and may have very much increased in the succeeding time. And besides all this, the tribes Asher, Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh are indeed more feebly represented than Zebulun, but more strongly than Naphtali. There therefore remains no reason for doubting the historical accuracy of the numbers given; but it is of course to be understood that the numbers, which are stated only in hundreds, are not the result of an enumeration of the individual persons, but only of an estimate of the various detachments according to the military partition of the tribes. <div eID="gen5715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5716" type="x-p"/> In regard to להסב מ, cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.10.14">1Ch 10:14</reference>; and as to יהוה כּפי, see the remark on יהוה כּדבר,   <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.3">1Ch 11:3</reference>, 1Ch 11:10.
